CITY OF PASADENA
  City Council Minutes
  November 23 2020-2:00 P.M.
  City Hall Council Chamber

  SPECIAL MEETING
  The virtual meeting was convened pursuant to Executive Order N-29-20 issued by
  Governor Gavin Newsom on March 17, 2020, and was held solely by
  videoconference/teleconference

  OPENING:  Mayor Tomek called the special meeting to order at 2:01 p.m. The
  pledge of allegiance was led by Mayor Tomek.

  ROLL CALL:  Mayor Terry Tomek
  Council members:  Vice Mayor Tyron Hampton
  Councilmember Victor Gordo
  Councilmember John J. Kennedy
  Councilmember Steve Madison
  Councilmember Gene Masuda
  Councilmember Margaret McAustin
  Councilmember Andy Wilson

  Staff:  City Manager Steve Mermell
  City Attorney/City Prosecutor Michele Beal Bagneris
  Assistant City Clerk Latasha Reese

  CEREMONIAL MATTERS  Mayor Tomek presented a proclamation declaring November 28,
  2020 as "Small Business Saturday," in the City of Pasadena .
........ .
  Mayor T ornek requested that the meeting be adjourned in memory
  of those that have suffered due to death and illness caused by
  COVID-19 in Pasadena, the nation and around the world .

  SPECIAL ITEM -COVID-19  COVID-19 UPDATE FROM CITY MANAGER AND PUBLIC
  HEALTH OFFICER

  Steve Mermell, City Manager, provided introductory comments, and
  Dr. Ying Ying Goh, MD, Director of Public Health, and Or. Matt
  Feaster, City Epidemiologist, reported on the COVID-19 pandemic,
  providing information on the number of cases and deaths ,
  hospitalizations and ICU admissions occurring in Pasadena , as well
  as at state and national levels, with all responding to questions. Dr.
  Goh provided update on the State's limited Stay at Home Orders;
  and expressed concerns with the alarming rate of increased Covid-
  19 cases. Dr. Lori Morgan, President of Huntington Hospital,
  provided information related to COVID-19 patients at the hospital;
  and responded to questions.

  Vice Mayor Hampton stated the following for the record, "That is
.......  also my hope, that we do not have to make a step that is detrimental
  to .. . as we had a ceremonial matter that was right before this ... to
  our small businesses, not necessarily just to small businesses. But

  Council Minutes  11/23/2020
   also the people who work in these businesses, they need the jobs,
  they need work, they need to be able to continue to pay their
  mortgages, they need to continue to pay their rent. This I
  understand, you know it is very serious, but it is an economic ... it's
  going to be an economic nightmare for the next three or four years
  and if the State is saying that you can still have outdoor
  dining ... unless the State is telling us to close it, I would advise that
  the City of Pasadena continue, no matter what. At this point
  following the County is ... if the State says that we could do it [allow
  outdoor dining] that is what we should be doing. And if the State
  says we can't do it, well then OK, then that's the fight. We have our
  Health Department and I know that we've had this over and over
  and gone over this over and over again, but at this point unless you
  can track all. .. you know a significant amount of cases happening to
  people doing outdoor dining or in store shopping, you know Target
  or Walmart or small business. At the end of the day, what I see here
  happening is ... this is an equity issue because people that are
  extremely wealthy are sitting and its fine for them because this is an
  economic boom for them. The Jeff Bezos' of the world ... the
  Amazon's of the world, the Walmart's, the Target's. This is an
  economic boom for them, but for the rest of America, which is 47%
  as the Mayor mentioned employed by small businesses, are
  suffering. And everyone in government, no offense to Dr. Goh , and
  everybody and Steve, you guys are all getting a check. No matter
  we close down or not, the City [of Pasadena] is still paying people.
  That's not a shot at you, I'm just saying outside of the City, there
  are people that live in the City that make our City what it is, and if
  they cannot afford to live in our City, wh ich they are already getting
  close to that because they are not able to work, then it's not Covid
  that has done this to us, it is government that his stifled people and
  forced them out of the City of Pasadena and closed businesses in
  the City of Pasadena. So unless the state is saying ... ! have to
  reiterate this ... unless the state says that we need to close those
  businesses, we can 't choose and pick because there is a surge. We
  have to let our businesses open and if you have to be more strict
  with our businesses and tell them , you know, they need to take a
  temperature every time somebody comes in, then do that. But we
  need to let our businesses open and they've invested a lot of
  money, a lot of money during Covid, and all of a sudden were going
  to tell them they have to close. And these people who don't know
  where they are going to get their next check from that live in our
  City. And now they have to go home and figure it out, potentially
  lose their homes. This is bigger ... speaking of the deaths, imagine
  the mental. .. people will. .. I'm just saying ... people will either
  continue to work and just say forget what was talked about at this
  point because the only right we have as Americans, is the right to
  work. That's a right and government does not have the right to tell
  me I can't work."

Council Minutes  2  11/23/2020
   Councilmember Kennedy stated the following for the record, "Dr.
  Morgan did you say elective surgery are being continued? Share
  with us exactly what you stated." Mr. Kennedy spoke on the need
  to allow science and data to lead the City's actions; and asked the
  City Attorney to determine if the City Council has the authority to
  use Water and Power funds to provide some level of protective
  equipment to the public.

  In response, Dr. Morgan replied that Huntington Hospital is within
  their capacity to manage the hospitals current patient volume, but if
  a surge becomes similar to the volume in March or July, the hospital
  will have to scale back in terms of surgeries.

  Councilmember Madison spoke on the need for additional COVID-
  19 testing resources, and asked staff to provide information on the
  City's website related to COVID-19 testing locations. He spoke in
  favor of not imposing additional stricter regulations related to dining
  or any other segment of the City's economy; and requested that an
  emergency meeting of the City Council be scheduled prior to any
  decisions made related to imposing stricter regulations to the City's
  businesses. He also spoke on the need for the Health Department
  to be robust and aggressive, including provide funding for COVID-
  19 vaccinations to the public.

  Councilmember Masuda asked staff to consider other options to
  help the restaurants, suggesting extending takeout hours.

  Councilmember McAustin spoke on the need for the underserved
  community, which has been negatively affected the most by
  COVID-19, to be given some priority when it comes time to
  administer the COVID-19 vaccination.

  Councilmember Wilson expressed concerns with the closing of City
  restaurants that would lead to individuals losing their jobs close to·
  the holidays; and spoke on the need for creative thinking to keep
  restaurants open during the COVID-19 pandemic.

  Councilmember Gordo requested that staff clarify the restaurant
  operating hours as there may be some confusion on that matter. He
  also asked staff to provide additional information on the percentage
  of current COVID-19 cases that are children under the age of 18 in.
  the last week or two to determine data on the surge of COVID-19
  cases. He asked staff to develop a COVID-19 vaccination
  distribution program taking into consideration the actions of the
  State and Los Angeles County related to the matter, suggested that
  staff provide an update to the Public Safety Committee.
  Councilmember Gordo requested that staff inform the Los Angeles
  County Board of Supervisors on the City's decision to assess data
  prior to closing restaurants in the City.

  Councilmember Kennedy expressed concerns with the Arroyo Seco
  Habitat Restoration project, specifically the lack of removal of
  Eucalyptus and Canary Island trees as he believes the trees are not
  safe. He also requested that the vendor, G Team Landscape
  Construction, Inc., hire young residents of Northwest Pasadena to
  assist with work related to the contract.

  In response to Councilmember Kennedy's request related to
  information on G Team Landscape Construction, lnc.'s principals,
  staff stated they would provide the City Council with a copy of the
  organization's Tax Payer Protection Act (TPA) form.

  Vice Mayor Hampton echoed concerns related to the Arroyo Seco
  Habitat Restoration project, specifically the lack of removal of
  Eucalyptus and Canary Island trees, which he believes may cause
  damage to the area. He spoke on the need for staff to review the
  City's policy to determine if invasive trees cause harm to the local
  ecology.

  Mayor Tomek asked staff to ensure the Eucalyptus and Canary
  Island Pine trees will be removed in the Lower Arroyo Seco once
  the native Sycamore trees have flourished in the area; and any
  Eucalyptus trees that provide a safety hazard will be removed.

  Following discussion, it was moved by Councilmember Madison,
  seconded by Councilmember McAustin, to approve the staff
  recommendation, amended to direct staff to ensure the Eucalyptus
  and Canary Island Pine trees will be removed in the Lower Arroyo
  Seco once the native Sycamore trees have flourished in the area:
